Chapter 10
Concerning the Way in Which the Strength of All Principalities Ought to Be Measured

When evaluating these principalities, you must consider another point. You need to ask whether a prince has enough power to stand on his own in times of need, or if he always has to rely on others for help. To be clear, a prince can support himself if he has enough men and money to raise a strong army and fight anyone who attacks him. On the other hand, a prince must rely on others if he cannot face his enemy in the open field and is forced to hide behind city walls for defense. We have already discussed the first situation, and we will return to it later. As for the second situation, the only advice is to tell these princes to fortify and stockpile supplies in their towns, and to completely abandon defending the surrounding countryside. If a prince builds strong defenses for his town and manages his subjects well, as I have advised before, his enemies will be very cautious about attacking him. Men hate to take on tasks that look difficult. No one thinks it is easy to attack a well-fortified town ruled by a prince who is not hated by his people.

Look at the cities of Germany. They are totally free, even though they control very little land around them. They only obey the emperor when it suits them, and they do not fear him or any other nearby powers. This is because they are fortified so heavily that everyone knows taking them by force would be a long, exhausting struggle. They have deep ditches, strong walls, and plenty of artillery. They also keep their public storehouses filled with enough food, drink, and firewood to last a whole year. Furthermore, to keep the people calm and avoid draining the state treasury, these cities always provide work for the public. They employ citizens in the trades that keep the city alive and strong, allowing the people to support themselves. They also highly value military training and have strict laws in place to maintain it.

Therefore, a prince with a strong city who has not made himself hated will simply not be attacked. Even if someone is foolish enough to try, the attacker will only be forced to retreat in disgrace. The affairs of this world are unpredictable, making it nearly impossible for an enemy army to sit idle and maintain a siege for a whole year. You might argue that if the people own property outside the city and watch it burn, they will lose patience. You might think a long siege and their own self-interest will make them turn against their prince. To this, I answer that a strong and courageous prince will easily overcome these challenges. He will give his subjects hope that the trouble will not last long. He will remind them of the enemy's cruelty to keep them fearful. At the same time, he will cleverly manage anyone who starts acting too bold or rebellious.

Furthermore, the enemy will naturally burn and ruin the countryside the moment they arrive. This happens when the citizens' spirits are still hot and they are eager to fight, so the prince has no reason to hesitate or worry. After some time passes and their spirits cool down, the damage is already done and cannot be reversed. At that point, the people will be even more eager to unite with their prince. They will feel he owes them a debt, since their houses were burned and their property was destroyed in his defense. It is human nature to feel bound to others as much by the favors we do for them as by the favors we receive. Therefore, if a wise prince considers everything carefully, he will have no trouble keeping his citizens loyal and determined from the beginning of a siege to the end, as long as he makes sure they have enough food and weapons to defend themselves.
